title: What a share is
summary: Ownership, dividends, votes, and why the price moves
body:
A share is a small slice of ownership in a company. If a company were split into a billion equal pieces, one share would be one of those pieces.

Owning one gets you three things. A claim on the profits, often paid out as dividends. A vote at the annual meeting. And a price that rises or falls as investors change their minds about what the company's future profits are worth.

Companies sell shares to raise money. The first time a company does this publicly is an IPO (initial public offering). Anthropic filed for one this week. After that, shares trade between investors on a stock exchange, and the company only sees the money from that first sale.

The price you see is simply the last price two people agreed to trade at. That is why it moves all day.

One UK quirk to learn early: London prices are usually quoted in pence, written p or GBX. SSE at 2,485p is £24.85 a share.
quiz_q: SSE shares closed at 2,485p on Monday. What is one share worth in pounds?
quiz_explain: UK prices are in pence, and 100p is £1, so divide by 100: 2,485p is £24.85.

title: How a stock market works
summary: Exchanges, buyers and sellers, and the bid–ask spread
body:
A stock market is simply a place where people who want to sell shares meet people who want to buy them. Today that place is a computer system run by an exchange, such as the London Stock Exchange or Nasdaq in New York.

The exchange doesn't set prices. It keeps an order book: a live list of everyone offering to sell, and at what price, and everyone wanting to buy, and at what price. When a buyer and a seller agree, a trade happens, and that price becomes the latest share price.

So at any moment there are two prices, not one. The bid is the most anyone is currently willing to pay. The ask (or offer) is the least anyone is willing to sell for. The ask is always a little higher than the bid, and the gap between them is called the spread.

Here's a real example from this morning. Hargreaves Lansdown showed SSE at 2,489p to sell and 2,491p to buy. The spread is 2p, under 0.1% of the price. If you bought and immediately sold, you would lose that 2p a share before the price had moved at all.

Big, busy shares like SSE, Microsoft or the global tracker funds have tight spreads because huge numbers trade every day. Smaller, quieter shares can have spreads of 1% to 5%, which quietly eats into returns.

Who makes sure there is always someone to trade with? Firms called market makers stand ready to buy and sell all day, and the spread is how they get paid.

Markets also keep hours. London trades from 8:00 to 16:30 UK time and New York from 14:30 to 21:00 UK time. Prices can still move outside those hours: Enphase fell about 16% in after-hours trading last night after its results, so a share can open far from where it closed.

For a long-term investor the lesson is simple. The spread is a hidden cost each time you trade, so trading less, and sticking to busy shares and funds, keeps more of your money working.
quiz_q: SSE is quoted at 2,489p to sell and 2,491p to buy. What is the spread?
quiz_explain: The spread is the gap between the buying and selling prices: 2,491p minus 2,489p is 2p.

title: Indices
summary: What the FTSE 100 and S&P 500 actually measure
body:
An index is a single number that tracks the prices of a basket of shares, so you can see in one glance how a whole market did. The FTSE 100 follows the 100 biggest companies listed in London; the FTSE 250 follows the next 250; the S&P 500 follows 500 large US companies.

The number itself (10,694 for the FTSE 100 last night) has no meaning on its own. What matters is how it changes: a 1% rise in the index means the basket, on average, rose about 1%.

Most big indices use market-cap weighting. A company's market cap is its share price times the number of shares, so giants count for much more than minnows. In the S&P 500, a handful of tech giants like Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia and Alphabet make up a large slice of the index. When they move, the whole index moves.

Wednesday showed why it pays to know which index you're looking at. On Budget day the FTSE 100 inched up 0.1%, helped by banks (relieved the new bank tax was smaller than feared) and SSE, up 4.6%. But the FTSE 250 fell 0.3%, because it holds more UK-focused firms such as housebuilders, which slid 6-7%. Same country, same day, different story.

In the US, the S&P 500 rose 0.3% even though Nvidia fell 1.2%. Because it's weighted by size, the gains elsewhere in big tech outweighed it.

Indices also matter because you can buy one. A tracker fund simply copies an index. VWRP, for example, follows the FTSE All-World index of about 4,000 companies worldwide.

Two things to remember: an index tells you about the average, not about your own shares; and most indices you see quoted ignore dividends, so they slightly understate what investors actually earned.
quiz_q: On Wednesday the FTSE 100 rose 0.1% but the FTSE 250 fell 0.3%. What's the best explanation?
quiz_a: One of the indices was calculated wrongly
quiz_b: They hold different companies: the FTSE 250 has more UK-focused firms like housebuilders, which fell
quiz_c: The FTSE 250 only trades in the afternoon
quiz_d: Indices always move in opposite directions
quiz_explain: Each index tracks its own basket of shares, so on a day when housebuilders slumped and big banks rose, the two could easily go different ways.

title: Funds, ETFs and investment trusts
summary: Buying hundreds of companies in one go
body:
Buying one share means betting on one company. A fund lets you buy a small slice of hundreds or thousands of companies in a single purchase. Your money is pooled with other investors' and the fund holds the shares for all of you.

A tracker fund (or index fund) simply copies an index, like the FTSE 100 or a world index. There is no star manager picking shares, so fees are low. V3AB, for example, is a tracker of thousands of companies worldwide, and VWRP tracks a similar world index. The fee you pay each year is the OCF (ongoing charges figure), often well under 0.3%.

An ETF (exchange-traded fund) is a fund that trades on a stock exchange like a share, so its price moves all day. INRG, a clean-energy fund, is an ETF. It owns about 100 clean-energy companies, including Enphase. When Enphase crashed 16% on Wednesday, INRG fell only 1.5%: losses in one company are softened by the rest. On Thursday Enphase bounced 3.5% and INRG barely moved.

An investment trust is different again. It is a company listed on the stock market whose business is owning other assets. Greencoat UK Wind and TRIG are investment trusts that own wind farms and solar parks. Because a trust has a fixed number of shares, its share price can drift away from the value of what it owns, its NAV (net asset value). When the share price is below NAV, it trades at a discount; above, at a premium. On Thursday Greencoat published its latest NAV, and TRIG finished selling its stake in the Beatrice offshore wind farm. That is the kind of news that can narrow or widen a trust's discount.

Thursday also showed how a broad fund behaves. Alphabet fell nearly 13%, its worst day on record. Yet V3AB slipped only 0.8% and VWRP 0.6%, because Alphabet is a small slice of each.

The trade-off: a fund spreads your risk, but you also give up the chance that one brilliant pick makes you rich. For most long-term investors that is a good swap.
quiz_q: Why did INRG fall only about 1.5% on the day Enphase, one of its holdings, crashed 16%?
quiz_a: INRG's managers sold Enphase before the fall
quiz_b: Enphase is only one of about 100 companies in the fund, so the others cushioned the drop
quiz_c: ETFs are protected from losses by the stock exchange
quiz_d: INRG is priced in pence, which makes falls smaller
quiz_explain: A fund spreads your money across many companies, so one company's crash moves the whole fund much less.

title: Why diversify
summary: Why one share is riskier than a hundred
body:
Diversification means spreading your money across many different investments so that no single one can do too much damage. The old saying is "don't put all your eggs in one basket", and Friday gave a perfect real-world demonstration.

On Friday Intel, one of the best-known chip companies in the world, fell 28.6% in a single day after giving a disappointing forecast. Anyone with most of their money in Intel lost more than a quarter of it before the weekend. Yet the S&P 500, which contains Intel alongside 499 other companies, fell only 1.8%. Intel is a tiny slice of that index, so its crash was cushioned by everything else.

The same thing showed up elsewhere. ASML fell 6.1%, Schneider Electric 4.1% and Nvidia 4.2%. But a broad global fund like the Vanguard ESG Global All Cap fund (V3AB) dropped 1.9%, because it owns thousands of companies in dozens of countries and industries. Meanwhile AstraZeneca jumped 7%. On any given day some things go up and others go down, and a diversified portfolio lets them partly cancel out.

There's a catch worth knowing: diversification only works if your investments don't all move together. Owning ten chip companies isn't really ten separate bets, because they tend to rise and fall as a group (investors call this being highly correlated). On Friday nearly every chip stock fell at once. True diversification means mixing different industries, regions and types of investment.

Diversification also has a cost: it caps your upside. If you'd put everything in AstraZeneca, Friday would have been brilliant. But nobody knows in advance which share will be the winner, and research shows most individual shares do worse than the overall market over long periods, while a few big winners do most of the heavy lifting. Owning the whole market makes sure you hold those winners.

That's why many investors build around a broad global fund with smaller tilts. The tilts add interest and the chance to beat the market; the core fund makes sure a bad day for one industry never becomes a disaster.
quiz_q: On Friday Intel fell 28.6% but the S&P 500 fell only 1.8%. What best explains the difference?
quiz_a: Intel is not part of the S&P 500
quiz_b: The S&P 500 holds 500 companies, so one company's crash is a small part of the total
quiz_c: Index funds are protected from losses
quiz_d: The S&P 500 only contains defensive companies
quiz_explain: Intel is in the S&P 500, but as one small slice among 500 companies its 29% fall barely dented the whole index.

body:
In investing, "risk" usually means something more specific than "the chance of losing everything". It mostly means uncertainty: how widely an investment's value might swing around before you need the money. The usual name for those swings is volatility.

This week was a good live example. On Wednesday Microsoft jumped 6.7% in a single day and Nvidia fell 3.2%. Brent crude, the oil price, dropped 8.7%. Meanwhile a broad global fund like Vanguard's ESG Global All Cap moved about 1.4%. Same day, same news, very different sizes of move.

Why the difference? A single company's price reacts to everything about that one business: its results, one big customer, one political decision. A fund holding thousands of companies averages those surprises out, so its daily moves are usually smaller. Single shares, themed funds and commodities are generally more volatile than broad funds.

Two useful ideas follow. First, a drawdown (how far something falls from its peak) is the number that tests your nerve. A share that is volatile can easily fall 30% or more from its high at some point, as ITM Power and Enphase have over the past year. Second, volatility is not the same as permanent loss. A fund that drops 10% and then recovers has cost you nothing unless you sold at the bottom.

That is why investors talk about risk tolerance: how much up-and-down you can sit through without panicking. Your time horizon matters a lot here. Money you need in a year should not be riding on volatile shares; money for twenty years from now can usually ride out several bad patches.

The VIX, often called the "fear gauge", measures how much volatility traders expect in US shares over the next month. It fell 20% on Wednesday to 16.6 as the election uncertainty cleared, a sign that the market's nerves had calmed. A VIX around 12-20 is ordinary; above 30 usually means real fear.

The practical lesson: expect swings, size them to your time horizon, and judge an investment over years rather than days.
quiz_a: Funds are not allowed to rise more than 2% a day
quiz_b: The fund holds thousands of companies, so big moves in single shares are averaged out
quiz_c: Microsoft is not included in global funds
quiz_d: Funds only update their prices once a week
quiz_explain: A broad fund spreads its money across thousands of companies, so one share's big jump or drop is a small slice of the whole, which keeps its swings smaller.
quiz_q: On Wednesday Microsoft rose 6.7% while a broad global fund rose about 1.4%. What best explains the smaller move in the fund?
summary: What a 2% drop in a day really means
title: Risk and volatility

body:
Most people judge an investment by its price: it was 100p, now it's 110p, so it's up 10%. But many shares and funds also pay you cash along the way, in the form of dividends. Total return adds the two together: the change in price plus any income you received, as a percentage of what you paid.

The sum is simple. Say a share costs 1,000p, rises to 1,050p over a year and pays 40p in dividends. The price return is 5%. The income return is 4%. The total return is 9%. Leave the dividends out and you would underrate it by almost half.

National Grid, which reported half-year results on Thursday, shows why this matters. Its shares closed at 1,285.5p. Over the past year it paid two dividends, 16.35p last November and 32.14p in May, about 48.5p in all, or roughly 3.8% of today's price. It also announced a new interim dividend of 16.97p. For a steady company like this, dividends can be a big slice of what investors earn over time.

Thursday also showed the other side. Nvidia fell 9.3% in a day and pays almost no dividend, so its return depends nearly entirely on its price. Growth companies tend to keep their profits to reinvest; mature ones such as utilities tend to pay them out. Neither is better: they are just different ways of delivering a return.

Over decades the gap compounds. If you reinvest dividends (use them to buy more shares), each payment buys more shares that pay dividends of their own. That is why long-run charts use adjusted prices that add dividends back in, and why long-run charts for shares and funds are often shown as total-return figures.

Funds handle this in one of two ways. Accumulating funds, often marked "Acc", reinvest the income for you, so the price already includes it; the Vanguard FTSE All-World fund VWRP works this way. Distributing funds pay the cash out instead, so their price alone understates what holders have earned.

The habit to build: when you compare two investments, ask "total return, or price only?" A share that has gone nowhere for five years but paid 4% a year has still made you about a fifth more money.
quiz_explain: The price rose 50p (5%) and the dividends added 40p (4%), so the total return is 90p on 1,000p, or 9%.
quiz_q: A share rises from 1,000p to 1,050p over a year and pays 40p in dividends. What is its total return for the year?
summary: Price moves plus dividends
title: Total return

body:
Compounding is what happens when your returns start earning returns of their own. In the first year, growth comes only from the money you put in. In the second year, it comes from that money plus last year's gains. Given enough time, the gains on gains end up bigger than anything you added yourself.

A simple example. Put £5,000 into a fund and suppose it grows by 6% a year on average (an illustration, not a forecast). After 10 years it is worth about £8,950. After 20 years, about £16,040. After 30 years, about £28,720. The second decade adds more than the first, and the third adds more than the first two together, even though you never added another penny.

That is why time matters more than timing or clever picking. Someone who starts ten years earlier gives compounding an extra decade to work on every pound, and a smart share pick rarely makes up for that. A handy shortcut is the rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly growth rate to get roughly how many years it takes to double your money. At 6% that is about 12 years; at 3%, about 24.

Compounding only works if the returns stay invested. Reinvesting dividends (Friday's lesson on total return) is one part of that. Keeping costs low is another, because fees compound too, in the wrong direction.

This week shows the catch: compounding is a long-run average, not a smooth line. The S&P 500 closed on Friday about 5.7% below its record of 7,818.93 from 6 October, after its worst day since April 2025 on Thursday and a small bounce on Friday. Long-run averages already include plenty of weeks like this. Selling after a bad week stops the clock, and it often means missing the rebound days that do much of the work.

The habit to build: think in decades, not days. When a bad week comes, ask how it looks on a 20-year chart. The long-run charts on the Stock Desk are a good place to practise.
quiz_explain: 72 divided by 8 is 9, so money growing at 8% a year roughly doubles in about 9 years.
quiz_q: Using the rule of 72, roughly how long does money take to double if it grows by 8% a year?
summary: Why starting early matters more than picking well
title: Compounding and time

body:
Every investment has costs, and they come off your return whether the market goes up or down. That makes them one of the few things you control.

There are a few main kinds. A platform fee is what the app or broker charges to hold your investments, often a percentage of your investments each year or a flat monthly fee. A fund's ongoing charge (OCF) is taken inside the fund every year; for a global tracker it is often well under 0.3%. The spread is the gap between the price you can buy at and the price you can sell at, a hidden cost each time you trade. Then there are taxes and fees on the purchase itself.

Here is how they add up on a £5,000 example spread across shares and funds. Buying £300 of a UK share such as SSE costs £1.50 extra, the 0.5% UK stamp duty on UK shares (UK-listed funds such as ETFs don't pay it). £300 of a US or Dutch share might cost £0.45, a 0.15% currency (FX) fee for swapping pounds into dollars or euros. A large French company such as Schneider Electric would cost £1.65: the FX fee plus France's 0.4% tax on buying large French companies. Many funds cost nothing to buy. In all, a few pounds on £5,000, under 0.1%.

One-off costs like these are small. The ones to watch are yearly charges, because they compound against you. Take £5,000 growing 6% a year for 30 years (an illustration, not a forecast): it ends at about £28,700. Knock 1% a year off in fees and it ends at about £21,600, roughly £7,100 less, for the same investment.

Trading often adds up too. Each round trip pays the spread and any fees again. Monday was a good test: after a rough week, shares jumped 2.4% in a day. Someone who sold in last week's fall and bought back on Monday would have paid costs twice and missed part of the bounce.

The habit to build: before buying anything, add up the yearly charges (platform plus fund) and the one-off costs, and compare them with a cheap global tracker.
quiz_explain: Buying shares in a UK company carries 0.5% stamp duty; there's no currency swap, and France's tax applies only to large French companies.
quiz_q: You buy £300 of shares in a UK company (not a fund) through a UK platform. Which extra cost applies to that purchase?
summary: Platform fees, fund fees, spreads, stamp duty and FX
title: Costs

body:
An ISA (Individual Savings Account) isn't an investment in itself. It's a wrapper: a container you put investments inside so the taxman leaves them alone. The shares and funds are the same; only the tax treatment changes.

In a stocks and shares ISA, any rise in value is free of capital gains tax (tax on the profit when you sell), and dividends are free of income tax. You can put in up to £20,000 each tax year (6 April to 5 April), across all your ISAs combined. Unused allowance doesn't roll over, so it's 'use it or lose it'.

Outside a wrapper, investments sit in a general investment account (GIA). There you get a small dividend allowance (£500 a year) and a capital gains allowance (£3,000 a year); above those, tax is due. That sounds plenty for a £5,000 investment, but compounding changes the picture. Over 20 or 30 years an investment can grow to many times what went in, and a gain of more than £3,000 in one year becomes easy to reach.

Take an example from this week. SSE reports half-year results on 18 November, and utilities like it pay out a large share of their profits as dividends. Held in a GIA, those payments count towards the £500 allowance; in an ISA they simply arrive tax-free and can be reinvested. The same goes for the income paid out by funds.

Two other wrappers are worth knowing. A Lifetime ISA (opened between 18 and 39) adds a 25% government bonus on up to £4,000 a year, but it's meant for a first home or retirement and carries a penalty if you take money out for anything else. A SIPP (self-invested personal pension) gives tax relief on the way in but locks money away until your late 50s; a later lesson compares pensions and ISAs.

A few practical points. Most platforms let you open a stocks and shares ISA with small amounts. You can move an ISA to another provider without losing its tax status, as long as you use the official transfer process rather than withdrawing the cash. And the wrapper doesn't protect you from losses: a share that falls 5.5% in a day, as Nvidia did on Tuesday, falls just as far inside an ISA. The wrapper shields your gains from tax, not from the market.
quiz_a: None: gains inside an ISA are tax-free
quiz_d: It depends on how many dividends were paid
quiz_explain: Gains and dividends inside an ISA are free of UK tax, so the £3,000 capital gains allowance only matters for investments held outside a wrapper.
quiz_q: You put £5,000 into a stocks and shares ISA and years later sell it all for £12,000. How much capital gains tax is due on the £7,000 profit?
summary: Keeping gains and dividends tax-free
title: ISAs and tax wrappers

body:
A company's results are its report card. Listed companies publish them every three or six months, and the share price often moves more on results day than on any other day of the quarter.

Start with revenue (the money taken in from sales). Then look at profit, often shown as operating profit (before interest and tax) and as earnings per share (profit divided by the number of shares). The operating margin tells you how much of each pound of sales is left after running costs: a rising margin usually means the business is getting more efficient or has pricing power.

Next, read the forward-looking parts. Guidance is what the company expects for the rest of the year. Orders and the order backlog (work already ordered but not yet delivered) hint at future sales. These often matter more than the past quarter, because the share price is about the future.

Vestas, the Danish wind turbine maker, showed this on Wednesday. Its third-quarter revenue rose 6% to €5.7bn, its operating margin improved to 8.5% from 7.8%, earnings per share hit a record and its order backlog reached a record €78bn. Yet the shares fell 3.8%. Why? New turbine orders dropped 27%, with no offshore orders at all, and extra costs on one offshore project hit the figures. Investors had expected more, and they care about where the business is heading.

That is the key lesson: the market reacts to results compared with expectations, not on their own. Analysts publish forecasts beforehand, and a company can grow nicely and still see its shares fall if it misses them, or shrink and see them rise if things were feared to be worse. CoreWeave rose about 25% on the same day because its sales beat forecasts and it raised its outlook.

As a long-term investor you don't need to trade on results day. But reading a results summary, even just the headline numbers, guidance and orders, helps you understand a company and why its share price moves.
quiz_c: Its order backlog hit a record
quiz_explain: Share prices look ahead, and fewer new orders point to weaker sales in future, which worried investors more than a good quarter just gone.
quiz_q: Vestas reported record earnings per share on Wednesday, yet its shares fell 3.8%. Which part of its report best explains the fall?
summary: What a company's quarterly report tells you
title: Reading results

body:
Every results announcement leads with three kinds of number: revenue, profit and margins. Learn these and most results headlines start to make sense.

Revenue (also called sales or turnover) is all the money a company takes in from customers. It's the "top line", because it sits at the top of the income statement. Growing revenue shows people want more of what the company sells, but on its own it says nothing about whether the company makes money.

Profit is what's left once costs are paid, and it comes in layers. Gross profit takes off the direct cost of making what was sold. Operating profit also takes off running costs such as wages, rent and marketing. Net profit (the "bottom line") is what's left after interest and tax as well. Companies often add adjusted profit figures that strip out one-off items. These can be useful, but the company chooses what to leave out, so notice when they're used.

A margin turns profit into a percentage of revenue. If a shop sells £100 of goods and makes £10 of operating profit, its operating margin is 10%. Margins let you compare companies of different sizes, and show whether a business is getting more or less efficient over time. Vestas, last lesson's example, lifted its operating margin from 7.8% to 8.5%: more of each euro of sales became profit.

Burberry showed all three on Thursday. Its revenue rose 6% on a year earlier, and it made an adjusted profit before tax of £27m in the first half, against a loss of £11m a year before. Sales grew a little, but profit swung a lot. That's because many costs, such as shops, staff and design, stay roughly fixed: once sales cover them, extra sales flow mostly into profit. Its shares rose about 8%.

The same effect works in reverse, which is why profits often fall faster than sales in a downturn. When you read results, check all three: is revenue growing, is the company actually profitable, and is its margin rising or falling?
quiz_explain: Operating margin is operating profit divided by revenue: £30m ÷ £200m = 15%, so 15p of every pound of sales is left after running costs.
quiz_q: A company's revenue is £200m and its operating profit is £30m. What is its operating margin?
summary: The three numbers in every results headline
